headline: Board reviewed measles and cyclosporiasis outbreaks, opioid settlement funds, Hepatitis C outreach, and rising Welfare Department costs; approved August 2026 minutes.
summary: The Board heard reports on rising measles cases nationwide, cyclosporiasis cases in New Hampshire, and respiratory illness trends. Staff reported on opioid settlement funds, the planned Resource Center at 45 High Street, Hepatitis C outreach, Environmental Health inspections, and increased Welfare Department expenditures. The Board approved the August 2026 minutes.

through leadership and community collaboration. Our vision  is to have an informed, safe, healthy, and

Epidemiologist 
Report 
Presented by 
Sakshi Gurung 
 The United States is experiencing an increase in measles cases, with approximately 
2,903 confirmed and suspected cases reported across 47 states as of September 3, 
2026, the highest total in 35 years. The increase is attributed to both interstate and 
local transmission, declining MMR vaccination rates, and an increase in travel-
related imported cases.
Page 2 of 4 
 
 Respiratory illness levels remain low, with emergency department visits at 
approximately 0.1%. 
 As of September 3, 2026, New Hampshire has reported 100 cases of cyclosporiasis 
and three hospitalizations. Of these, 45 cases were domestically acquired and 
associated with the recalled product, 48 were domestically acquired with an 
unknown source, and seven were associated with international travel. 
 Wastewater testing for influenza, COVID-19, and RSV is being done. 
Director’s Report  
Presented by  
Bobbie Bagley, 
Director DPHCS  
 DPHCS vision and mission were read.  
Financial Update 
 Nashua received $146,000 from the State Treasurer as a part of the opioid 
settlement fund to the State of NH subdivisions. 
 Approximately $446,000 is currently available in the trust fund. The Director made 
a request was made to the Mayor for $150,000 to support the Warming Station. 
Community partners have applied for grants. There are two partner awaiting 
award approval. 
 The Board of Aldermen is expected to consider approval of the Resource Center at 
45 High Street location of Harbor Care at the upcoming meeting on Thursday, 
September 10, 2026. The legislation for the Gap Analysis Committee for the 
Resource Center is also on the agenda. 
 Community Health Workers (CHWs) had 245 client interactions this past month. A 
client success story involving an 18-year-old unhoused individual was discussed. 
Staff made calls to identify housing options for youth, and were able to assist with 
finding housing through an organization. 
 The Housing Services Officer (HSO) has been involved in Resource Center activities, 
including the rental TBRA program and related meetings. 
 Health Promotion and Communication Specialist activities included developing 
Hepatitis C cards and a Back-to-School event. 
 Public Health Emergency Preparedness activities include CPR and First Aid training 
scheduled for the month of September -Preparedness month, for City Employees. 
 Part-time staff positions have been posted for the Resource Center and Per Diem 
positions are posted for the Warming Station. 
 A question was raised regarding the approximately $446,000 balance and the 
proposed $150,000 allocation for the Warming Station. It was noted that the 
department does not spend the entire balance of the Opioid Abatement Trust Fund 
because the timing of the next installment is uncertain. 
 The State allocates 15% of the Abatement Trust Fund Settlement funds to 22 
subdivisions. Approximately 85% of the funds received by the State is granted out 
to support agencies providing prevention, treatment and recovery services, 
including police and fire departments. Communities are required to demonstrate  
using funds for opioid abatement activities.

Department 
Report

 A new vaccine cooler has been received, with capacity to store approximately 100 
vaccines. 
 Approximately 1,500 people attended the Back-to-School event attended by staff.

 Lead outreach continues with Lamprey and other organizations, including lunch-
and-learn sessions and distribution of educational materials. 
 Annual Competency Day was completed as part of licensing requirements. 
 Fit testing has been completed. 
 A new per diem staff member has joined the department. 
 Two staff members completed infection-control certification. 
 The Hepatitis C Coordinator discussed the goal of reaching  people where they are and 
providing treatment in community settings. Staff are working with organizations such as 
SSANA and other facilities to identify and treat individuals who may otherwise have 
difficulty accessing care. Testing and medications are brought directly to facilities when 
possible. Medications can also be delivered to the department. The program has gained 
good momentum, with increasing compliance and approximately six positive cases 
identified on average each month. Clients are advised at the four-week mark about 
changing personal-use items to help prevent reinfection. It was discussed that the Hepatitis 
C virus can remain on surfaces for an extended period, potentially up to six weeks. 
Questions/Comments 
 A question was raised regarding genotype testing. Current guidelines do not recommend 
routine genotype testing; however, Well Sense requires genotype testing. 
 The program is funded through Opioid Abatement Trust Fund because the Hepatitis C cases 
being addressed are associated with opioid use. 
 A question was asked about whether family practices can receive informational flyers. It 
was confirmed that flyers are available and will be distributed. 
Environmental 
Health (EH) 
Department 
report provided 
by Deputy Health 
Officer –Mike 
McGuiness 
Environmental Health reported a busy month with the following activities: 
 Several inspection failures were reported, with follow-up site visits conducted. 
 Complaints regarding rodents and hygiene were addressed. 
 One license was suspended for nonpayment. 
 Two emergency calls were received, and two businesses voluntarily closed. 
 Temporary events were particularly busy. 
 Septic system work continued. 
 One school inspection was completed. 
 The department did not meet its goal of completing all scheduled inspections due 
to staff shortage.  
 A couple of pool closures occurred. 
 No positive rabies cases were reported. 
 The department continued work related to the lettuce recall. 
 Environmental Health is working with other City departments regarding displaced 
residents and expects to have increased involvement in these cases. Several 
departments met following a fire at a hoarder property. Legal training was 
completed regarding RSA 147 and the displacement protocol. Housing, Fire, and 
Building Departments are working together on displacement cases, including 
reviewing applicable codes and RSAs. The application of certain codes and RSAs to 
owner-occupied properties remains challenging and may present legal issues. 
Questions/comments
Page 4 of 4 
 
 A question was raised about whether the legal process changes when a child or 
elderly person is living in the home. It was explained that the process does not 
change when the child or elderly person is a family member of the property owner. 
However, concerns can be reported to Child Protective Services or the Bureau of 
Elderly and Adult Services when appropriate. 
 A question was raised regarding the previously approved software. 
 The new software has been included in the budget for installation and 
maintenance; however, additional funding will be needed for full implementation. 
Welfare 
Department 
report provided 
by Mike 
Amichetti,  
Welfare Specialist 
Supervisor 
 August expenditures were approximately $94,000, compared with $78,000 in 
August of the previous year, an increase of approximately $16,000. 
 The number of applicants has also increased. 
 Shelter remains the largest expense, at approximately $86,000, which is about 
$10,000 higher than last year. 
 Utility assistance showed the largest increase, with approximately three times as 
many vouchers issued compared with the previous year. A total of 57 vouchers 
were issued for rent or motel costs. 
 Overall assistance numbers have increased. Approximately 47% of applicants 
received assistance, which is higher than last year. 
 The department assisted three families and two individuals before they were 
referred to shelter. 
 The Welfare Department updated its financial standards to reflect increases in the 
cost of living. The updated standards are available on the City website. 
 Total Welfare expenditures for July and August were approximately $135,000, 
resulting in a slight budget overage. 
 The department continues to maintain relationships with community partners and 
service organizations. 
Other Updates  
 Discussion was held regarding appointing another Board of Health member to replace Dr. 
Stephanie Wolf Rosenblum. Appointment of the new member will come from the 
Mayor’s Office  
Public Comment
